meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Owen's essay. Why am I here?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
A machine's guess. The company that sells it says not to use it alone. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now, what do you have on the essay itself?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. Owen wrote it over the weekend, so he could have drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in. Does this document show anything else?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Pasting would look the same, yes. I'm reading 3.2 now. Students misquote; a wrong line is a mistake, not proof of anything.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and an essay. That's called revising. Is that all of it?

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
A boy put on the spot after class says "like, being stuck," and you call that evidence. Is any of this on his record right now?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Fine. A private rewrite, to put this behind him, and not because he did anything. In writing tonight, with nothing on his record.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, then. Until then, the zero comes off the gradebook, and Owen hears the plan from me, not from his phone.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, Hale. A private rewrite Thursday, the zero off the gradebook until then, nothing on his record, all in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed to a private supervised rewrite of Owen's essay on Thursday, November 12 after school under procedure 4.4, with its mark replacing the zero, nothing placed on his record, and the mark entered well before December 1. I still require the zero removed from the gradebook until then, and that Owen hears this plan from me and not from his phone. I expect it in writing tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private, supervised rewrite on Thursday with nothing on his record, and she still wants the zero off the gradebook until then and to tell Owen herself; that is the fair outcome under 4.4, and her time did not run out first.
What moved her: You owned entering the zero before calling home, in one sentence, and moved on, because it answered her main grievance about procedure and got her to listen to your evidence.
What cost ground: You opened by calling the checker score conclusive, because she treated it as a machine's guess and shut down until you set it aside.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history, with the document created at 11:31 PM the night before it was due, came closest to that night, though it proves nothing about the essay itself and is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked whether anything was on his record right now, answer that directly before moving on to your offer.
